m-sternocleidomastoideus.summary: A prominent muscle running obliquely across the side of the neck and dividing it into anterior and posterior triangles. It has two heads: sternal and clavicular.
facts: Sternal head: front of the manubrium of the sternum; clavicular head: upper surface of the medial 1/3 of the clavicle
Outer surface of the mastoid process and lateral half of the superior nuchal line
Accessory nerve (XI) – motor; C2–C3 – proprioceptive
Occipital, superior thyroid and suprascapular arteries

One side: tilts the head to the same side and turns the face to the opposite side and upwards; both sides: flex the head forwards and, with the head fixed, raise the sternum as accessory muscles of respiration
clinical: Injury or fibrosis of the muscle at birth causes congenital torticollis (wry neck).
Accessory nerve injury weakens turning the head to the opposite side.
tus: SCM divides the neck into anterior and posterior triangles; the accessory nerve emerges into the posterior triangle at the middle of its posterior border (near Erb's point).
In congenital muscular torticollis the head tilts towards the lesion and the face turns to the opposite side.

mm-scaleni.summary: Three muscles running from the transverse processes of the cervical vertebrae to the first two ribs. The brachial plexus and subclavian artery pass through the gap between the anterior and middle scalenes.
facts: Tubercles of the transverse processes of C2–C7
Anterior and middle: 1st rib (anterior scalene to the scalene tubercle); posterior: 2nd rib
Anterior rami of the cervical nerves (C3–C8)
Ascending cervical artery (inferior thyroid artery), transverse cervical artery
Raise the first two ribs to assist inspiration; bend the neck to the same side
sections: The phrenic nerve descends on the front of scalenus anterior. The subclavian vein passes in front of this muscle; the subclavian artery and brachial plexus pass behind it (through the scalene gap).
clinical: Compression in the scalene gap or a cervical rib can cause thoracic outlet syndrome (numbness of the arm, weak pulse).
The interscalene block is used to anaesthetise the brachial plexus for shoulder surgery.
tus: Scalenus anterior runs from the anterior tubercles of the C3–C6 transverse processes to the 1st rib; the phrenic nerve passes in front of it, the subclavian artery behind.
The scalenes raise the 1st and 2nd ribs in forced inspiration.

mm-suprahyoidei.summary: Four muscles above the hyoid bone that form the floor of the mouth: digastric, stylohyoid, mylohyoid and geniohyoid.
facts: Digastric: posterior belly from the mastoid notch, anterior belly from the digastric fossa; stylohyoid: styloid process; mylohyoid: mylohyoid line; geniohyoid: inferior mental spine
Hyoid bone (the intermediate tendon of digastric via a fibrous loop)
Anterior belly of digastric and mylohyoid: nerve to mylohyoid (V3); posterior belly of digastric and stylohyoid: facial nerve (VII); geniohyoid: C1 (carried by the hypoglossal nerve)
Submental artery (facial artery), lingual artery, occipital artery
Raise the hyoid and larynx in swallowing; with the hyoid fixed they depress the mandible and open the mouth
tus: The suprahyoid muscles pull the hyoid and larynx upwards in swallowing and also help open the mouth.
Mylohyoid forms the floor of the mouth (oral diaphragm); the submandibular gland wraps around its posterior border.

mm-infrahyoidei.summary: Four strap-like muscles below the hyoid bone: sternohyoid, omohyoid, sternothyroid and thyrohyoid.
facts: Sternohyoid and sternothyroid: back of the manubrium of the sternum; omohyoid (inferior belly): superior border of the scapula; thyrohyoid: oblique line of the thyroid cartilage
Hyoid bone (sternothyroid: thyroid cartilage)
Ansa cervicalis (C1–C3); thyrohyoid: C1 (with the hypoglossal nerve)
Superior thyroid artery, lingual artery
Pull down and steady the hyoid and larynx during swallowing and speech
clinical: In thyroid surgery these muscles are retracted; the ansa cervicalis is preserved where possible.
tus: The intermediate tendon of omohyoid crosses in front of the internal jugular vein and is anchored to the clavicle by a fascial sling.
In thyroidectomy the infrahyoid ('strap') muscles are separated in the midline to expose the gland.

mm-prevertebrales.summary: Deep flexor muscles of the neck lying on the front of the cervical vertebrae.
facts: Longus colli: vertebral bodies and transverse processes of C3–T3; longus capitis: transverse processes of C3–C6
Longus colli: anterior tubercle of the atlas and upper cervical vertebrae; longus capitis: basilar part of the occipital bone
Anterior rami of the cervical nerves (C1–C6)
Vertebral artery, ascending cervical artery
Flex the neck and head; support the cervical lordosis
clinical: The deep neck flexors are often strained in whiplash injuries.
tus: Longus colli and capitis flex the neck; they can be strained in whiplash injury.
The 'danger space' between the prevertebral fascia and these muscles is a route by which infection can spread into the mediastinum.

m-trapezius.summary: A broad superficial muscle over the upper back and back of the neck; together with its partner it forms a diamond (hood) shape. It has upper (descending), middle (transverse) and lower (ascending) parts.
facts: Superior nuchal line, external occipital protuberance, nuchal ligament, spinous processes of C7–T12
Lateral 1/3 of the clavicle, acromion and spine of the scapula
Accessory nerve (XI) – motor; C3–C4 – sensory
Transverse cervical artery (superficial cervical artery), suprascapular artery, occipital artery
Upper fibres elevate the scapula (shrugging) and rotate it upwards; middle fibres retract it; lower fibres depress it and assist upward rotation
clinical: If the accessory nerve is injured in the posterior triangle during cervical lymph node biopsy, the shoulder droops and the arm cannot be raised above 90°.
The shoulder shrug test assesses the accessory nerve.
tus: Trapezius: upper fibres elevate the scapula, middle fibres retract it, lower fibres depress it; upper and lower fibres together rotate it upwards.
Its sensory (proprioceptive) fibres come from C3–C4; its motor nerve is the accessory nerve.

m-latissimus-dorsi.summary: The broadest muscle in the body, covering the lower and lateral back. It forms the posterior wall of the axilla.
facts: Spinous processes of T7–L5, thoracolumbar fascia, posterior 1/3 of the iliac crest, lower 3–4 ribs, inferior angle of the scapula
Floor of the intertubercular sulcus of the humerus
Thoracodorsal nerve (C6–C8)
Thoracodorsal artery (subscapular artery)
Extends, adducts and internally rotates the arm (climbing, rowing); with the arm fixed it pulls the trunk upwards
clinical: In breast reconstruction the muscle can be used as a flap together with its vascular pedicle.
Thoracodorsal nerve injury during mastectomy weakens adduction and internal rotation of the arm.
tus: Latissimus dorsi lifts the trunk when walking on crutches.
In breast reconstruction the latissimus dorsi flap is raised on the thoracodorsal vessels.

mm-rhomboidei.summary: Two muscles beneath trapezius running between the vertebral column and the medial border of the scapula.
facts: Minor: lower part of the nuchal ligament, spinous processes of C7–T1; major: spinous processes of T2–T5
Medial border of the scapula (minor at the level of the spine, major between the spine and the inferior angle)
Dorsal scapular nerve (C4–C5)
Dorsal scapular artery (deep branch of the transverse cervical artery)
Retract, elevate and rotate the scapula downwards; hold the scapula against the chest wall
tus: In rhomboid palsy the medial border of the scapula drifts slightly outwards; it is tested by pressing the hands on the hips.

m-levator-scapulae.summary: A muscle on the posterolateral neck running from the upper cervical vertebrae to the superior medial angle of the scapula.
facts: Posterior tubercles of the transverse processes of C1–C4
Upper part of the medial border of the scapula (between the superior angle and the spine)
Dorsal scapular nerve (C5) and C3–C4 spinal nerves
Dorsal scapular artery, transverse cervical artery
Elevates the scapula and rotates it downwards; bends the neck to the same side
clinical: Tension in this muscle is a common cause of neck pain and stiffness in desk workers.
tus: Levator scapulae is a common cause of neck pain and torticollis; it is supplied by C3–C4 and the dorsal scapular nerve.

mm-serrati-posteriores.summary: Thin muscles in the intermediate layer of the back that attach to the ribs; they play an accessory role in respiration.
facts: Superior: nuchal ligament, spinous processes of C7–T3; inferior: spinous processes of T11–L2
Superior: upper borders of ribs 2–5; inferior: lower borders of ribs 9–12
Superior: intercostal nerves 2–5; inferior: intercostal nerves 9–11 and subcostal nerve
Posterior intercostal arteries
Superior raises the ribs, inferior pulls the ribs down (contributing to respiratory mechanics)
tus: Serratus posterior superior assists inspiration, the inferior assists expiration by pulling the ribs down; both are supplied by intercostal nerves.

m-erector-spinae.summary: The largest of the deep (intrinsic) back muscles, running along both sides of the vertebral column. From lateral to medial it consists of the iliocostalis, longissimus and spinalis columns.
facts: Back of the sacrum, posterior iliac crest, lumbar spinous processes, sacrotuberous ligament and a common broad tendon
Iliocostalis: angles of the ribs and transverse processes of the lower cervical vertebrae; longissimus: transverse processes, ribs and mastoid process; spinalis: upper spinous processes
Posterior rami of the spinal nerves
Posterior intercostal, lumbar and lateral sacral arteries
Both sides: extend the spine and head (upright posture); one side: lateral flexion to the same side; works eccentrically to control forward bending
clinical: Acute low back pain (lumbago) is often linked to spasm of this muscle group.
Strengthening this muscle group is the basis of rehabilitation in chronic low back pain.
tus: Erector spinae consists, from lateral to medial, of the iliocostalis, longissimus and spinalis columns ('I Love Spine').
It controls forward bending of the trunk by eccentric contraction; spasm occurs in low back pain.

mm-transversospinales.summary: Deep back muscles running from the transverse processes of the vertebrae to the spinous processes above: semispinalis, multifidus and rotatores. Splenius and the short segmental muscles (interspinales, intertransversarii, levatores costarum) are also studied with this group.
facts: Transverse processes of the vertebrae and the sacrum
Spinous processes of higher vertebrae (semispinalis capitis to the occipital bone)
Posterior rami of the spinal nerves
Posterior intercostal, lumbar and occipital arteries
Extend the spine and rotate it to the opposite side; provide segmental stability between vertebrae (especially multifidus)
clinical: Atrophy of lumbar multifidus is associated with chronic low back pain.
tus: Semispinalis, multifidus and rotatores belong to this group; multifidus is an important muscle for lumbar stability.

mm-suboccipitales.summary: Four small muscles between the base of the skull and the first two cervical vertebrae: rectus capitis posterior major and minor, obliquus capitis superior and inferior.
facts: Rectus major and obliquus inferior: spinous process of the axis; rectus minor: posterior tubercle of the atlas; obliquus superior: transverse process of the atlas
Inferior nuchal line of the occipital bone (obliquus inferior to the transverse process of the atlas)
Suboccipital nerve (posterior ramus of C1)
Vertebral artery, occipital artery
Extend the head and rotate it to the same side; make fine postural adjustments
sections: The vertebral artery and suboccipital nerve lie in the floor of the triangle bounded by rectus capitis posterior major and obliquus capitis superior and inferior.
tus: The suboccipital muscles are supplied by the suboccipital nerve (posterior ramus of C1); C1 usually has no sensory branch.
The greater occipital nerve (posterior ramus of C2) emerges at the lower border of the suboccipital triangle; it is involved in occipital neuralgia.

m-pectoralis-major.summary: A large fan-shaped muscle covering the upper front of the chest; it forms the anterior wall of the axilla. It has clavicular, sternocostal and abdominal parts.
facts: Clavicular part: medial half of the clavicle; sternocostal part: sternum and costal cartilages 1–6; abdominal part: aponeurosis of the external oblique
Crest of the greater tubercle of the humerus (lateral lip of the intertubercular sulcus)
Medial (C8–T1) and lateral (C5–C7) pectoral nerves
Pectoral branch of the thoraco-acromial artery, lateral thoracic artery, intercostal arteries
Adducts and internally rotates the arm; the clavicular part flexes, the sternocostal part extends the flexed arm; with the arm fixed it pulls the trunk up (accessory muscle of respiration)
clinical: In Poland syndrome the sternocostal part of the muscle is congenitally absent.
In heavy lifting (bench press) its tendon can tear off the humerus.
tus: Poland syndrome is the congenital absence of the sternocostal head of pectoralis major.
The anterior axillary fold is formed by pectoralis major, the posterior fold by latissimus dorsi and teres major.
